'''''Veronica salicifolia''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Hebe salicifolia''''',<ref name=POWO_812616-1/> the '''koromiko''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''willow-leaf hebe''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Plantaginaceae]], which is found throughout the [[South Island]] of [[New Zealand]] and in Chile. It is a large, evergreen shrub, reaching {{convert|2|m|spell=in}} in height, with light-green, spear-shaped leaves that are up to {{convert|12|cm|spell=in}} long, and white or pale lilac flowers.

==Description==
The overall form of ''V. salicifolia'' can be described as "willow-like" due to its drooping appearance, hence the name New Zealand willow.<ref name="Timber Press">Metcalf, L. (2006).Hebes. A guide to Species, Hybrids, and Allied Genera. Oregon: Timber Press.</ref> Unlike most Hebes that contain erect seeding structures, it has downward hanging capsules that disperse via gravity.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006">Bayley, J.M., & Kellow, V.A. (2006). An Illustrated Guide to New Zealand Hebes. New Zealand: Te Papa Press.</ref> ''V. salicifolia'' is one of the larger [[hebe (plant)|hebe]] species, its woody structure allowing it to grow to around one to five meters tall and it can have quite a wide spread foliage.  Its narrow, oblong shaped leaves are oppositely arranged and are a dark to yellowish green colour, they also have hairs situated on the mid rib of the leaf.<ref name="Timber Press"/> ''H. salicifolia''  is perennial and flowers in Summer and Autumn, producing<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.southlandcommunitynursery.org.nz/uploads/Southland%20plant%20ID%20-%20SCN%202015%20Plant%20Course.pdf|title=Southland Community Nursery.|access-date=2017-05-20|archive-date=2017-04-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170407101824/http://www.southlandcommunitynursery.org.nz/uploads/Southland%20plant%20ID%20-%20SCN%202015%20Plant%20Course.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> multiple white and/or violet flowers can be found clustered together on stems that grow up to {{convert|24|cm}} long.<ref name="Timber Press" /> It is also one of the few Hebes that have a pleasantly strong scent.  They also produce a generous amount of nectar in comparison to other Hebes.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006" /> Some of the less obvious structures that help distinguish it from other Hebes are its distinctive leaf buds, large nodules and shape and colour of its reproductive structures.  For example, the stamens are considered to be short and the anthers are violet in colour.<ref name="Timber Press" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Veronica salicifolia'' is found in Chile, the South Island of New Zealand, as well as the [[Stewart Island|Stewart]] and [[Auckland Islands]]. It has also been recorded as naturalised in Europe. As a form expressing a wide diversity in ecology and morphology, it inhabits regions from coastal margins to alpine regions up to {{convert|2800|m}} above sea level, which is regarded to be the highest place for a flowering plant in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=515|title=NEW ZEALAND PLANT CONSERVATION NETWORK: Veronica salicifolia.}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Scoparia rotuella female.jpg|thumb|left|New Zealand moth ''S. rotuella'', known to pollinate ''V. salicifolia'']]
''Veronica salicifolia'' attracts a wide range of unspecialized and promiscuous insects. Beetles and flies, especially syrphids, collect mainly pollen, whereas bees visited the flowers for both pollen and nectar, and tachinid flies and Lepidoptera primarily collect nectar. Especially at low altitudes, small native solitary bees and flies are common visitors.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006" />  More specific survey was made by Mark & Steve (2013), native butterflies of New Zealand have been feeding on nectar of Veronica spp. The New Zealand endemic moth ''Scoparia rotuella'' is known to pollinate this species.<ref>{{CiteQ| Q54669862}}</ref> As shown in the laboratory test, its flowers significantly increased the fitness of female butterflies.<ref name="Butterfly Breeding Guide">{{Cite web|url=http://www.forestandbird.org.nz/files/file/Butterfly%20Manual.pdf|title=Butterfly Breeding Guide.|access-date=2017-05-20|archive-date=2017-04-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170417042727/http://forestandbird.org.nz/files/file/Butterfly%20Manual.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Australasian green shield bugs often sit their egg shells on a wide variety of native and naturalised trees and shrubs including Koromiko. Adults and juveniles of Australasian green shield bugs feed by inserting a stylet into the plant and then suck plant sap and berries.<ref>[https://nzacfactsheets.landcareresearch.co.nz/factsheet/InterestingInsects/Australasian-green-shield-bug---Glaucias-amyoti.html Interesting Insects & other Invertebrates.] Australasian green shield bug - Glaucias amyoti.</ref> As for diseases, leaf spot and downy mildew may occur in poor condition.<ref name="Metcalf L. J. 2001">Metcalf L. J. (2001). International register of hebe cultivations. Canterbury: The Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture.</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Veronica salicifolia'' is thought to be one of the first New Zealand hebe species to be described by the English during [[James Cook|Captain Cook]]'s second voyage in 1773, by botanist [[Georg Forster]] and his father [[Johann Reinhold Forster]]. Hebes found up North in the [[Waitākere Ranges]] were once mistaken for it due to their similar white and violet flowers, these are now distinguished as separate locally endemic Hebe.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006" />

==Cultivation==
''Veronica salicifolia''  is a hardy plant but is not tolerant of shade and needs to be in grown in full sun and in a sheltered area with a well drained soil. It can, however, tolerate wet areas and can often be found on the edge of bush and wetlands.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006" />

Once established, they have considerable drought tolerance<ref name="Bayly M. 2006">Bayly M., Kellow A. (2006) An illustrated guide to New Zealand hebes. Wellington: Te Papa Press. </ref> and also have been found to be tolerant of freezing. In the test, 50% damage to leaves was reported at {{convert|-0.6|C}}. Technically, ''H. salicifolia'' has closed vegetative buds, which could give protection from frost by covering the vulnerable apex, and only open when fully grown.  However, Dallimore (1913) pointed that most Hebe is only specialized in habitats similar to New Zealand. Hebe may not be hardy except when grown in the southern and western countries of England, the west of Scotland, Ireland and various islands off the west coast of Britain.<ref name="Metcalf L. J. 2001" />

==In Māori culture==
Before the English conquest, the [[Māori people|Māori]] had been utilizing the plants medicinal properties for centuries.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006" /><ref name="maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz">Ngā Tipu Whakaoranga database. (2017). Plant Use Details, Hebe salicifolia, Hebe stricta and similar spp. Koromiko. Kōkōmuka. Main reference Retrieved from https://maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz/WebForms/PeoplePlantsDetails.aspx?PKey=5B284386-E5E5-40D3-B677-5094A18152B6</ref> The leaves were chewed to help cure diarrhoea and applied to the skin to aid ulcers and wounds.<ref name="maoriplantuse.landcareresearch.co.nz" /> ''Koromiko'' is the general name for the hebes in the [[Māori language]] and is shared over a range of New Zealand Hebe species such as the [[Veronica elliptica|shore koromiko]] (''Veronica elliptica'') and varnished koromiko (''[[Veronica vernicosa]]''), for example.<ref name="Bayley, J.M. 2006" />
